newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Markets cower as U.S. payrolls loom.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Markets cower as U.S. payrolls loom.

text.p: A heavy-hitting U.S. employment report will hang over financial markets in the week ahead, forcing other economic news into the shadows.
But before that report hits on Friday, markets will digest inflation figures in France, Italy and Germany, real economy data from Britain and Germany and U.S. December producer prices.
"The payrolls data will dominate," said Keith Edmonds, senior analyst at IBJ International in London.

Recent data -- including a stronger-than-expected National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index released on Thursday -- have cast doubt on the view that the U.S. economy had slowed towards trend growth at the close of last year.
"It looks actually as if the U.S. economy gained momentum going into the end of 1996," Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said.
"And if the employment report confirms that scenario, it will maintain pressure on U.S. bond and equity markets, and probably the dollar as well," he said.

IBJ's Edmonds said he expected a rise of around 160,000 in December non-farm payrolls, compared with 118,000 in November, but some analysts said the figure may be bloated by seasonal hiring for the Christmas period in the retail sector.
For bond investors, another major factor in the near term week will be a full plate of supply as markets open up to the new year.
The glut of new paper may prove difficult for markets to absorb, analysts said.
"Bond markets can expect a slightly sour tone to the beginning of the new year," said Edmonds. "There may well be some short-term indigestion."

German debt prices may be the hardest hit, with the issue of as much as 15 billion marks of 10-year Bunds due in the first 10 days of January. Analysts said redemptions coming up across global markets should ensure cash is available for investment, but said players may not be ready to put funds to work straight away, preferring to wait for a more definitive 1997 trend to be established in world markets.
Although European data will be somewhat overshadowed by the U.S. jobs report, analysts said markets would be keeping a keen eye on some major releases.

Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer in London, said manufacturing new orders numbers for Germany due before Tuesday, and final price data from Italy, would provide some European interest.
The first estimate of German 1996 gross domestic product will come on Thursday, and should underline speculation that growth remains soggy for the moment, analysts said.

IBJ's Edmonds said he expected economic growth to have been around 1.4 percent in Germany in 1996, adding that this would imply a weak fourth quarter. "Concerns about weak growth in Europe are going to persist," he said.
German jobless numbers, coupled with French and German inflation data, should confirm that core European economies are struggling.
In Britain, provisional M0 money supply, due for release on Monday, is expected to have slowed slightly to 0.7 percent in November versus a 0.8 percent gain in the previous month.
But analysts said that if the figure was much higher than forecast, speculation will heat up that monetary policy will have to be tightened again soon.
Britain also sees November industrial production and manufacturing output data on Friday.
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
